div.head: MEMB. 6. SUBSECT. 1.

Against Envy, Livor, Emulation, Hatred,
Ambition, Self-love, and all other affections.
div.p: Against those other Qui invidiam ferre non potest, ferre contemptum cogitur [He who cannot bear envy is forced to bear contempt].passions & affections, there is no better remedy, than as Mariners when they go to Sea, provide all things necessary to resist a tempest; to furnish ourselves with Philosophical & Divine precepts, other men’s examples, Ter. Heautont.Periculum ex aliis facere, sibi quod ex usu siet [make the trials of others useful for yourself]: to balance our hearts with love, charity, meekness, patience, and counterpoise those irregular motions of envy, livor, spleen, hatred, with their opposite virtues, as we bend a crooked staff another way, to oppose Epictetus cap. 14.sufferance to labour, patience to reproach, bounty to covetousness, fortitude to pusillanimity, meekness to anger, humility to pride, to examine ourselves for what cause we are so much disquieted, on what ground, what occasion, is it just or feigned? And then either to pacify ourselves by reason, to divert by some other object, contrary passion, or premeditation. Ter. Phor.Meditari secum oportet quo pacto adversam aerumnam ferat, Pericla, damna, exilia peregre rediens semper cogitet, aut filii peccatum aut uxoris mortem, aut morbum filiae, communia esse haec: fieri posse, ut ne quid animo sit novum [We should reflect on how to bear hardship, danger, loss, exile, and that a man returning home from abroad should always expect his son to have transgressed, or his wife to have died, or his daughter to have become sick – that these things are universal, that they can happen – so that nothing will surprise his mind]. To make them familiar, even all kind of calamities, that when they happen, they may be less troublesome unto us. In secundis meditare, quo pacto feras adversa [In favourable times, consider how to endure adversity]; or out of mature judgement to avoid the effect, or disannul the cause, as they do that are troubled with toothache, pull them quite out.

l.hi: Ut vivat castor, sibi testes amputat ipse;

lg.l: Tu quoque siqua nocent, abjice, tutus eris.
The Beaver bites off’s stones to save the rest:
Do thou the like with that thou art opprest.

div.p: Or as they that play at wasters, exercise themselves by a few cudgels how to avoid an enemy’s blows: let us arm ourselves against all such violent incursions, which may invade our minds. A little experience and practice will inure us to it; vetula vulpes, as the proverb saith, laqueo haud capitur, an old Fox is not so easily taken in a snare: an old soldier in the world methinks should not be disquieted, but ready to receive all fortunes, encounters, and with that resolute Captain, come what may come, to make answer,

l.hi: O virgo nova mi facies inopinaque surgit,

lg.l: Omnia percepi atque animo mecum ante peregi.
No labour comes at unawares to me,
For I have long before cast what may be.
——— non hoc primum mea pectora vulnus
[… This wound is not the first my heart
Has felt; I’ve borne things more painful …]

div.p:
The Commonwealth of Nat. Chytraeus delitiis Europae.Venice, in their Armoury have this inscription, Happy is that city which in time of peace thinks of war, a fit Motto for every man’s private house; happy is the man that provides for a future assault. But many times we complain, repine and mutter without a cause, we give way to passions, we may resist, and will not. Socrates was bad by nature, envious, as he confessed to Zopyrus the Physiognomer, accusing him of it, froward and lascivious: but as he was Socrates, he did correct and amend himself. Thou art malicious, envious, covetous, impatient, no doubt, & lascivious, yet as thou art a Christian correct & moderate thyself. ’Tis something I confess, and able to move any man, to see himself contemned, obscure, neglected, disgraced, undervalued, Occupet extremum scabies, mihi turpe relinqui est [Let the scab take the last, for me it’s shameful to be left behind]. Hor.left behind, some cannot endure it, no not constant Lipsius, a man discreet otherwise, yet too weak and passionate in this, as his words express, Lipsius epist. quaest. lib. 1 ep. 7.collegas olim, quos ego sine fremitu non intueor, nuper terrae filios, nunc Maecenates & Agrippas habeo, ——— summo jam monte potitos [I have former colleagues, whom I can’t contemplate without rage, not long ago lowly good-for-nothings, now Maecenases and Agrippas … now occupying top spot]. But he was much to blame for it; to a wise staid man this is nothing, we cannot all be honoured and rich, all Caesars; if we will be content, our present state is good; and in some men’s opinion to be preferred. Let them go on, get wealth, offices, titles, honours, preferments, and what they will themselves, by chance, fraud, imposture, simony, and indirect means, as too many do, by bribery, flattery, and parasitical insinuation, by impudence, and time-serving, let them climb up to advancement in despite of virtue, let them go before, cross me on every side, Lipsius epist. lib. 1 epist. 7.me non offendunt modo in oculos incurrant, as he said, correcting his former error, they do not offend me, so long as they run not into mine eyes. I am inglorious and poor, composita paupertate [in tranquil poverty], but I live secure and quiet: they are dignified, have great means, pomp and state, they are glorious; but what have they with it? Gloria comitem habet invidiam, pari onere premitur retinendo ac acquirendo [Glory has envy as a companion; it’s equally burdensome to keep as it is to acquire].Envy, trouble, anxiety, as much labour to maintain their place with credit, as to get it at first. I am contented with my fortunes, spectator e longinquo [a long-distance observer],
and love Neptunum procul a terra spectare furentem [to gaze from the land on Neptune’s distant rage]: he is ambitious, and not satisfied with his: but what gets he by it? To have all his life laid open, his reproaches seen; not one of a thousand but he hath done more worthy of dispraise and animadversion, than commendation; no better means to help this than to be private. Let them run, ride, strive as so many fishes for a crumb, scrape, climb, catch, snatch, cozen, collogue, temporize and fleer, take all amongst them, wealth, honour, Et omnes fama per urbes garrula laudet [And let prattling fame praise him throughout every city].and get what they can, it offends me not:

lg.l: [… let my own land protect me
With a safe and secret dwelling,]

div.p: I am well pleased with my fortunes,

lg.l: [… I live and reign as soon as I’ve given up {what you exalt}.]

div.p:
I have learned in what state soever I am therewith to be contented, Philip. 4. 11. Come what can come, I am prepared, Nave ferar magna an parva, ferar unus & idem [carried by ship large or small], I am the same. I was once so mad to bustle abroad, and seek about for preferment, tire myself, and trouble all my friends, sed nihil labor tantus profecit; nam dum alios amicorum mors avocat, aliis ignotus sum, his invisus, alii large promittunt, intercedunt illi mecum solliciti, hi vana spe lactant; dum alios ambio, hos capto, illis innotesco, aetas perit, anni defluunt, amici fatigantur, ego deferor, & jam, mundi taesus, humanaeque satur infidelitatis acquiesco [but this drudgery achieved nothing; for while death called some of my patrons away, I was unknown and disliked by others; some made big promises, some were concerned and intervened on my behalf, and some led me on with false hope. Meanwhile as I cultivated them, gaining the favour of some, and becoming known to others, time was running out, the years flowing by, my patrons growing weary, and I was being dragged down; and now, tired of the world and glutted with the disloyalty of mankind, I give in]. And so I say still; although I may not deny, but that I have had some The right honourable Lady Frances Countess Dowager of Exeter. The Lord Berkeley.bountiful patrons, and noble benefactors, ne sim interim ingratus [lest I should be ungrateful meanwhile], and I do thankfully acknowledge it, I have received some kindness, quod Deus illis beneficium rependat [may God repay them for this help], si non pro votis, fortasse pro meritis, more peradventure than I deserve, though not to my desire, more of them than I did expect, yet not of others to my desert; neither am I ambitious or covetous, all this while, or a Suffenus to myself; what I have said, without prejudice or alteration shall stand. And now as a mired horse that struggles at first with all his might and main to
get out, but when he sees no remedy, that his beating will not serve, lies still, I have laboured in vain, rest satisfied, and if I may usurp that of Distichon ejus in militem Christianum, e graeco. Engraven on the Tomb of Fr. Puccius the Florentine in Rome. Chytraeus in delitiis.Prudentius,

lg.l: Nil mihi vobiscum, ludite nunc alios.
Mine haven’s found, fortune and hope adieu,
Mock others now, for I have done with you.
